column16: We annually report and release our consumption based emissions for London. Tackling the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from London's buildings, transport and industry is a huge challenge and well recognised by the Mayor of London. The impact of greenhouse gases goes far beyond the city's boundaries too and London has an important role to play in the global context. Understanding emissions from our consumption patterns can help us better understand and plan to reduce London's wider carbon footprint. Latest data available:https://data.london.gov.uk/dataset/london-s-consumption-based-greenhouse-gas-emissions?q=consumption%20based . We are also members of the C40 Consumption Based Emissions (CBE) Working Group, sharing knowledge and data with multiple cities globally. In addition to this, we also took part in a pilot project with C40 to develop some Actionable Data Indicators for CBE action in London. This leveraged our existing CBE database as well as some proxy datasets to help track the impact of interventions around CBE. We have recently also been working with C40 peers to discuss improvements to CBE emissions modelling, including how to analyse CBE inventories based on demographic data and other trends outside of spending.

column16: The city of Oslo just published the first set of indicators for indirect emissions: https://www.klimaoslo.no/klimabarometeret/. These will be used to trace the change in indirect, consumption-based emissions, i.e. procurement, mobility and food consumption. These include indirect emissions from the municipality's own consumption of goods and services and the municipality's own building projects, kg waste produced per capita, and the number of cars per capita. The data-quality for these indicators is high, and they reflect the city's most impactful means for tackling indirect emissions. The City of Oslo has conducted a full consumption-based inventory using the currently available data from Statistics Norway: https://www.klimaoslo.no/wp-content/uploads/sites/88/2018/12/Asplan-Viak-Forbruksbasert-klimaregnskap.pdf This inventory was done in 2018, mainly with data from 2012. Poor data quality, sporadic updates and lack of data indicate that an annual consumption-based inventory is not feasible at this point. The city has requested cooperation with several state agencies that have the jurisdiction and means to gather consumer purchase data, to establish routines for consumption-based reporting on a national level that follows the established routines for the direct emission accounting.

A consumption-based emissions inventory was developed for Copenhagen to assist in the development of goals and sub-goals for the coming Climate Strategy 2035, and in the identification of consumption hotspots to be addressed by actions in the first Climate Action Plan. This covered the period 2010 to 2021 and was derived from top-down, input-output methods. Private households' consumption footprint was estimated specifically for Copenhagen residents, while the climate footprints of capital investments and public consumption were scaled down (based on Copenhagen's share of residents in Denmark) from the national consumption-based inventory prepared annually by the Danish Energy Agency. 

In 2019, the average Copenhagen resident emitted approximately 10 tons CO2-e annually from a consumption-based perspective, distributed as follows: Newbuild and construction (buildings and other infrastructure) 14%, Housing (primarily energy consumption) 9%, Food and beverages 19%, Mobility/transportation 11%, Consumer goods 8%, Leisure and travels ,7%, Other private consumption 4%, Other capital investments 13%, Public consumption 15%. For further details see the technical note for the City's Technical and Environmental Committee on Copenhagen's consumption-based emissions (in Danish): www.kk.dk/sites/default/files/agenda/0beb135a-b4ee-4384-891a-fb94ab2e4b5a/2f3287f6-6ce2-4ed1-8e7f-9a7e41b83949-bilag-6_0.pdf

The strategy includes a goal of halving consumption-based emissions per citizen by 2035, compared to baseline year 2019. The strategy is expected to be finally adopted politically in autumn 2025 following a public hearing phase completed in summer 2025. Methods for developing an improved consumption-based emissions inventory are currently under development. This inventory will, as far as possible, use Copenhagen-specific data, such that it is responsive over for changes resulting from initiatives included in consecutive climate action plans.

Municipal Consumption Emissions:
City of Melbourne does not currently maintain an inventory of jurisdiction-wide emissions, however, consumption-based emissions were calculated and published in the Climate Change Mitigation Strategy to 2050 as additional to the BASIC method that is more accurate for the purpose of tracking emission reductions due to the availability of data. The City of Melbourne's consumption-based emissions for the calendar year 2011 were 3,114,928 tonnes CO2-e which was 28.19 tonnes CO2-e per person. The Climate Change Mitigation Strategy includes actions to reduce consumption based emissions by adopting circular economy principles to reduce the environmental impact and embodied emissions from products, materials and buildings across the city through procurement, urban design and planning and waste avoidance.

Corporate Consumption Emissions:
The City of Melbourne commits a significant budget to capital or infrastructure works every year. We are committed through our five-year Emissions Reduction Plan (ERP) 2021-26, the City to better understanding the embodied emissions in our infrastructure projects and assessing alternative materials which might reduce these emissions. Of the eight priorities in the ERP, number three is 'Measure and minimise embodied carbon in design and construction' Actions over the next five years:1. Prioritise low emissions criteria for new buildings.2. Minimise embodied emissions and maximise circular design principles in design and construction.3. Leverage contracting to deliver optimal low carbon outcomes. 

The City's Sustainable Assets Policy, including design specifications, implementation tool and accompanying technical guidance is currently still in development. When complete, it will ensure all assets are built with future climate scenarios in mind as well as meeting a host of new minimum environmental performance standards.

column16: The \'Carbon Footprint Inventory Report for Accommodation Service (per room per day) (Deluxe Classic Room - King Bed 10 pings)\' of InterContinental Kaohsiung Hotel is based on the requirements of the ISO 14067:2018 standard and “the Key Points for Promoting Product Carbon Footprint Management” by Taiwan's Environmental Protection Administration of the Executive Yuan(current name: Ministry of Environment) as per Attachment 3-2-3_AccommodationService. The hotel commissioned Afnor International Co., Ltd. to conduct external verification of the carbon footprint report. On-site verifications were carried out on May 21-24, 2024, and June 6-7, 2024, to confirm that the carbon footprint data complies with the Guidelines for Calculating the Carbon Footprint of Products and Services.\nThe inventory data is in Attachment 3-2-3_InterconinventoryS2. This inventory uses the life cycle assessment tool “SimaPro v9.4.0.2,” with the database “Ecoinvent 3” (in Attachment 3-2-3_SimaProFactors). The life cycle impact assessment methodology follows the IPCC 2021 GWP 100a (incl. CO2 uptake) v1.00 greenhouse gas emission evaluation method, calculating the carbon dioxide equivalent from raw material extraction to the waste stage (cradle to grave, B-2-C). For this service, InterContinental Kaohsiung Hotel provides the \'Deluxe Classic Room - King Bed (10 pings) per room per day\' accommodation service, and all greenhouse gas emissions are fully included in the calculation without excluding any items.\nHowever, the inventory belongs to the InterContinental Kaohsiung Hotel and hence is confidential, we cannot upload the inventory. The attachments include all supporting methods, carbon footprint report and 3rd party verification statements.

column16: A elaboração deste inventário seguiu o padrão internacional de melhores práticas - GPC - Global Protocol for Community-Scale (Protocolo Global para Inventários de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa na Escala Comunitária). A Metodologia GPC foi lançada em 2014 em parceria realizada entre o ICLEI Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade, World Resources Institute (WRI) e o Grupo de Liderança Climática C40, tendo como base os Manuais para Inventários de GEE Nacionais de 2006, publicados pelo IPCC, e com o suporte e aprovação do Banco Mundial, do Programa das Nações Unidas para os Assentamentos Humanos (ONU-Habitat) e do Programa das Nações Unidas para o Meio Ambiente (UNEP - United Nations Environment Program). A metodologia GPC oferece um padrão para organizar e relatar as emissões de GEE de cidades. Os principais conceitos contábeis da metodologia GPC incluem: 2. METODOLOGIA 2.1 A Metodologia GPC 15 a) a organização da quantificação das emissões em Setores e Subsetores; b) o conceito de Escopo, para diferenciar as emissões que ocorrem dentro e fora do limite geográfico da cidade; c) os diferentes Níveis de Reporte. Esta metodologia busca separar os dados de emissões para que sejam identificadas as maiores fontes de GEE em uma cidade, determinando seis diferentes setores, nos quais as atividades emissoras identificadas podem ser alocadas: Energia Estacionária; Transporte, Resíduos; IPPU (Industrial Processes and Product Use - Processos Industriais e Uso do Produto); AFOLU (Agriculture, Forest and Land Use - Agricultura, Floresta e Uso da Terra); e Outras Emissões Indiretas; cada um contemplando Subsetores, Os setores são agrupados dentro de três categorias de escopos, com base no local onde as atividades ocorrem, se dentro ou fora do limite da cidade. Os escopos ajudam a diferenciar as emissões que ocorrem fisicamente dentro dos limites da cidade (Escopo 1), daquelas ocorrendo fora da cidade (Escopo 3), e daquelas emissões indiretas provenientes da geração da energia elétrica, que apesar de geradas fora dos limites do município, são consumidas dentro das fronteiras geográficas do município (Escopo 2). Os Níveis de Reporte oferecem às cidades a opção de selecionar entre dois níveis de relato: BÁSICO ou BÁSICO+. A abordagem de nível BÁSICO contempla as fontes de emissão mais comumente observadas nas cidades, associadas aos setores Energia Estacionária, Transporte (ambos dentro do limite geográfico da cidade) e Resíduos. Isso permite que todas as cidades que utilizem a metodologia GPC sejam comparadas. Esta foi a opção adotada por Curitiba para este inventário. Além de reportar os GEE por Setores e Escopos, existem as emissões de CO2 que são resultado da combustão de biomassa. Essas emissões são denominadas Emissões Biogênicas, ou seja, provém de fluxos naturais de biomassa, seja vegetal ou animal, e são consideradas neutras em termos de impacto. Em outras palavras, este CO2 apresenta um ciclo biológico (e não um ciclo geológico, como o CO2 de origem fóssil), permanecendo pouco tempo na atmosfera e, portanto, não tendo impacto substancial no clima do planeta, Os dados de atividade são referentes ao consumo que geram emissões de GEE, por exemplo, consumo de energia elétrica e consumo de combustíveis. Já os fatores de emissão convertem os dados da atividade em emissões. O reporte das emissões é realizado em toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO2e). Esse valor é obtido multiplicando as emissões dos GEE inventariados pelo seu respectivo Potencial de Aquecimento Global (GWP - Global Warming Potential), valor publicado pelo IPCC, o qual representa o impacto variável de determinado GEE emitido para a atmosfera, Para o inventário de emissões de Curitiba ano-base 2016 foram utilizados os Potenciais de Aquecimento Global do Quarto Relatório do IPCC (publicado em 2007). Inventario de GEI de Cali (WWF-DAGMA, período 2016-2021) — descripción breve

Responsables: WWF Colombia junto con el Departamento Administrativo de Gestión del Medio Ambiente (DAGMA) de Cali, y participación de actores como empresas de servicios públicos, Secretaría de Movilidad, entidades regionales como la CVC, y organismos nacionales. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Alcance temporal: histórico de emisiones para los años 2016-2021. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Sectores cubiertos:

Transporte - incluye trayectos urbanos y viajes hacia/a los municipios vecinos. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Residuos - emisiones generadas por gestión de residuos sólidos y posiblemente aguas residuales. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Energía estacionaria - uso de energía en viviendas e industrias dentro de la ciudad. 
Gobierno de Caldas

AFOLU (Agricultura, Ganadería, Forestación y otros usos del suelo) - aunque su participación es menor en comparación con los anteriores. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Resultados principales para 2021:

Transporte fue el sector con mayor aporte, representando ≈ 43 % de las emisiones de CO₂ equivalente de la ciudad. 
Gobierno de Caldas

El sector residuos aportó alrededor del 35 %. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Energía estacionaria contribuyó con aproximadamente 22 %. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Importancia operativa:

Establece líneas base para que la administración de Cali identifique los sectores prioritarios donde intervenir para reducir emisiones. 
Gobierno de Caldas

Permite evaluar los efectos de la pandemia en las emisiones, mostrando descensos temporales o cambios en patrones de emisión que luego revirtieron cuando la ciudad retomó actividades. 


Incluye componente de fortalecimiento institucional: WWF entregó una herramienta metodológica para que Cali pueda continuar haciendo estos inventarios de forma más autónoma, con datos de entidades externas/internas.

column16: Wellington City's consumption-based GHG inventory for FY2019/2020 estimates total emissions at 1,392,000 tCO₂e, with households (46%), business capital (39%), and government (15%) as the primary contributors. This inventory uses the PAS 2070 standard, which allocates emissions based on the consumption of goods and services, including upstream emissions from production and transport, regardless of where they occur. The methodology combines spend-based data (e.g., card transactions) and physical data (e.g., electricity use), multiplied by emission factors derived from national sources like ThinkStep and AgriLink. Emissions from food and drink were the largest single category (23% of total), highlighting a key area for policy intervention. Compared to the city's production-based inventory, the consumption-based total is 33% higher, reflecting Wellington's role as a “consumer city.” The inventory supports Te Atakura - First to Zero, Wellington's climate action plan, by identifying high-impact areas for emissions reduction. Importantly, this inventory enables more informed decision-making by linking emissions to consumer behaviour and guiding targeted emissions reduction strategies.

Em 2019, as emissões por setor foram: Energia Estacionária - 717 ktCO2e (26%), Transportes - 1073 ktCO2e (40%), Resíduos e Efluentes - 792 ktCO2e (29%) e AFOLU - 121 ktCO2e (6%). No último ano estudado, o perfil de emissões por setor foi: Energia Estacionária - 661 ktCO2e (26%), Transportes - 866 ktCO2e (35%), Resíduos e Efluentes - 839 ktCO2e e AFOLU - 132 ktCO2e (6%). Destaca-se que o setor de transportes foi responsável pela maior emissão em todos os anos estudados (1.043 ktCO2e (2018), 1.073 ktCO2e (2019) e 866 ktCO2e (2020)), seguido pelo setor de resíduos (707 ktCO2e (2018), 792 ktCO2e (2019) e 699 ktCO2e (2020)). O setor de energia estacionária se configurou como o terceiro maior emissor (727 ktCO2e em 2018, 716 ktCO2e em 2019 e 682 ktCO2e em 2020). Com exceção do setor de AFOLU, todos os outros setores apresentaram uma queda em suas emissões em 2020, o que pode ser justificado pela pandemia de COVID-19. Impulsionado pelo desmatamento, o setor de AFOLU apresentou uma maior emissão em 2020 (132 ktCO2e), seguido pelo ano de 2018 (131 ktCO2e) e o ano de 2019 apresentou as menores emissões para o setor nos anos estudados (121 ktCO2e). Os cálculos de emissões seguiram os preceitos da abordagem Basic+ da metodologia GPC, levando em consideração os escopos 1, 2 e 3. Os setores analisados no estudo foram energia estacionária, transporte, resíduos e efluentes, e AFOLU. O setor de IPPU não foi incluído no estudo por falta de dados de atividades para o cálculo das emissões. As emissões totais do setor de Energia Estacionária foram calculadas levando em consideração as emissões relativas ao escopo 1 e 2. No escopo 1, foram calculadas as emissões da utilização de Gás Liquefeito de Petróleo (GLP) e da utilização de Óleo Combustível. As emissões relacionadas ao escopo 2 levaram em consideração o consumo de energia elétrica residencial, comercial, institucional, indústria, iluminação pública e fontes não especificadas. As emissões do setor de transporte foram calculadas a partir dos dados de compra de combustíveis no município (fuel sales approach). Para o cálculo das emissões, foram utilizados dados de venda de combustível dos subsetores de transporte rodoviário e aviação. As emissões relativas ao transporte ferroviário e fora das vias foram estimadas em conjunto ao subsetor de transporte rodoviário, uma vez que os dados de venda de combustível não discriminam quanto de combustível foi utilizado por cada modal. Os transportes aquáticos não ocorrem em grande volume e em sua maioria utilizam diesel como combustível, que foi considerado nos cálculos de transporte rodoviário. O transporte rodoviário representou o maior volume de emissão para o setor em todos os anos estudados. Para o setor de resíduos e efluentes foram calculadas as emissões relativas ao manejo de resíduos sólidos e ao tratamento de esgoto. Não ocorriam na cidade incineração ou tratamento biológico de resíduos. Os dados utilizados para o cálculo das emissões foram fornecidos pela prefeitura de Teresina. Para o cálculo das emissões dos resíduos sólidos foi usada a metodologia “compromisso com o metano” (Methane commitment), que leva em conta as emissões de todo o resíduo depositado por ano, mesmo que essas emissões não sejam liberadas nesse mesmo período. Em Teresina, o cálculo de emissão para o setor de Agricultura, Floresta e Outros Usos da Terra levou em consideração as emissões provenientes da fermentação entérica, do manejo de dejetos dos rebanhos, supressão de florestas, reflorestamento e do cultivo de arroz. As bases de dados utilizadas foram: dados da pecuária brasileira por município fornecidos pelo IBGE para o cálculo de fermentação entérica e manejo de dejetos, imagens de satélite para o cálculo de desmatamento, dados fornecidos pela prefeitura para o cálculo de remoção de CO2 a partir do de plantio de mudas e dados sobre a agricultura brasileira por município (IBGE) para o cálculo de emissões por plantações de arroz.

column16: In collaboration with Boulder County citywide consumption-based emissions were analyzed by EcoDataLab. The city's CBEI report is the first of its kind report for Boulder. The CBEI looks at emissions that occur anywhere in the world as a result of Boulder community members activities. It includes emissions not previously measured from categories such as food goods and services and underscores the importance of addressing our upstream emissions. Though the methodology behind this CBEI is different from other city emissions inventories there's a great deal of overlap between the two. The CBEI revealed that in 2021 the typical Boulder household was responsible for roughly 38 metric tons of CO2e annually MTCO2e or about 175 MTCO2e per person. With 42,376 households in the city this is a total of roughly 16 million MTCO2e in 2021 attributable to residents of Boulder. When compared with the city's traditional Community GHG Inventory, which shows a total carbon footprint of 14 million MTCO2e citywide, the CBEI helps broaden the picture of emissions attributable to Boulder residents. For the first time, data is available for the emissions categories of food goods and services. Transportation, food and services are the largest overall categories accounting for 31%, 20% and 19% of emissions, respectively. Together, these account for almost 70% of total emissions. Within subcategories gasoline, healthcare and electricity are the top three accounting for 21%, 10% and 7% of total emissions respectively, almost 40% combined.

Kota Medan saat ini belum memiliki inventarisasi emisi berbasis konsumsi penuh, namun laporan Inventarisasi Gas Rumah Kaca dan Rencana Aksi Mitigasi Perubahan Iklim Kota Medan Tahun 2023 telah menghitung emisi dari konsumsi energi rumah tangga, transportasi, dan limbah domestik. Perhitungan dilakukan dengan mengacu pada IPCC 2006 Guidelines menggunakan faktor emisi per kWh listrik, per liter BBM, serta volume limbah padat dan cair. 

Inventarisasi emisi di Kota Medan masih berbasis produksi (production-based), belum menggunakan pendekatan berbasis konsumsi (consumption-based). 
Saat ini inventaris berbasis konsumsi di Kota Medan baru mencakup energi, transportasi, limbah, dan sebagian industri. Belum masuk konsumsi barang & jasa lain (makanan, pakaian, produk impor).

Namun, ada beberapa bagian yang bisa dijadikan ikhtisar awal yang mengarah ke konsumsi:
 
1. Sektor Konsumsi Energi Rumah Tangga; sumber emisi adalah konsumsi listrik PLN, LPG untuk memasak; metode perhitungan yaitu Konsumsi energi × faktor emisi (kgCO₂/kWh listrik, kgCO₂/kg LPG) -` IPCC 2006.

2. Sektor Konsumsi Transportasi; sumber emisi adalah bahan bakar kendaraan pribadi & angkutan umum (BBM Besin dan solar); metode perhitungan yaitu Jumlah kendaraan × konsumsi rata-rata BBM × faktor emisi (kgCO₂/liter BBM) - IPCC 2006.

3. Sektor konsumsi limbah domestik; sumber emisi adalah sampah rumah tangga & limbah cair (IPAL domestik); metode perhitungan yaitu 
Volume limbah × faktor emisi CH₄/N₂O sesuai model IPCC (Tier 1).

4. Sektor konsumsi Industri (energi dan proses); sumber emisi adalah pemakaian energi industri dan emisi proses produksi; metode perhitungan yaitu Aktivitas produksi × faktor emisi energi/material - IPCC 2006.

It focuses on estimating emissions at a high spatial resolution through a hybrid approach, breaking down consumption into Demographic Statistical Areas (DeSO), thus enabling detailed insights into emissions linked to specific regions. The tool assesses both direct emissions, which occur during the use of products, and indirect emissions that arise throughout the supply chain. For more information of the methodology: https://www.sei.org/publications/consumption-compass-2-methods-data/

The Tool facilitates the use of community and regional-scale data sources, and in cases where local data is not available, assumptions or proxies are utilized. They are each evaluated by sector - residential, institutional, commercial, and light industrial ((I)CI).

column15: ADB Baguio Carbon Footprint.pdf,[CleanAirAsia] Final Report-Baguio Emissions Inventory Project-30July2022.pdf
column16:
The consumption-based inventory accounts for emissions from electricity consumption (Scope 2), fuel use for road transport, solid and liquid waste generation, and land use change. In 2018, Baguio's carbon footprint was 629,483 tCO₂e, or 1.76 tCO₂e per capita — 53% higher than the Philippine average ADB Baguio Carbon Footprint . Breakdown (2018):
  • Electricity consumption - 53.56% of total emissions (grid-supplied, linked to household and commercial demand).
  • Road transport - 20.04% (mainly jeepneys, buses, trucks).
  • Solid waste disposal - 13.01% (mostly biodegradable and food waste).
  • Liquid waste (sewage, septage) - 12.57%.
  • Land cover change (deforestation/urbanization) - 0.5-1%.
Methodology: The inventory applied the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and the Global Protocol for Community-Scale GHG Emission Inventories (GPC), adapted to Baguio's available datasets. National power generation data was proportionally attributed to Baguio based on electricity consumption. Transport emissions were calculated using vehicle registration, mileage, and fuel economy data. Waste emissions were estimated via the First Order Decay model. This approach reflects consumption-based emissions because it attributes electricity-related emissions, fuel used for goods/services, and waste disposal to end users in the city, rather than production sources outside the city.

Probolinggo City's official GHG inventory currently follows a production-based methodology, consistent with the GPC and IPCC guidelines. This approach captures all emissions occurring within the city's administrative boundary, including energy consumption, transportation, and waste.

However, the City recognizes that a consumption-based calculation provides an important complementary perspective. Under this approach, emissions embodied in imported electricity, food, construction materials, and other goods consumed in Probolinggo are included.

Preliminary analysis suggests that Probolinggo's consumption-based emissions are approximately 20-30% higher than production-based emissions, due to reliance on imported electricity and construction materials produced outside the city

column16:
Saat ini, Kota Manado belum memiliki konsumsi-based inventory (CBI) resmi yang terdokumentasi dalam laporan emisi atau RPJMD. Inventarisasi emisi yang ada masih berbasis production-based inventory (PBI) sesuai pedoman IPCC 2006 dan Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup dan Kehutanan, yakni menghitung emisi yang timbul dari aktivitas di dalam wilayah administrasi kota (energi, transportasi, limbah, pertanian, kehutanan).

Lingkup: mencakup jejak karbon barang dan jasa yang dikonsumsi masyarakat Manado, meskipun diproduksi di luar daerah (misalnya beras dari Minahasa, daging dari provinsi lain, barang impor, listrik dari sistem interkoneksi Sulawesi).

Metode yang bisa digunakan:
Environmentally Extended Input-Output Analysis (EE-IOA): untuk menghitung emisi dari rantai pasok barang/jasa berdasarkan data perdagangan antarwilayah.
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA): untuk menilai emisi sepanjang siklus hidup produk (produksi, transportasi, konsumsi, pembuangan).
Hybrid Approaches: kombinasi data inventarisasi lokal (misalnya konsumsi LPG/listrik rumah tangga, impor pangan) dengan faktor emisi nasional/global.

Manfaat: dapat memperlihatkan jejak karbon konsumsi kota yang lebih komprehensif, termasuk pola konsumsi rumah tangga, pariwisata, dan perdagangan.

Status saat ini: Sudah ada URL resmi atau publikasi dari Pemkot/Bapperida Manado terkait konsumsi-based inventory. Semua laporan yang tersedia (Inventarisasi GRK Kota Manado, RPJMD, KLHS) masih menggunakan pendekatan produksi.
Apakah Anda ingin saya buatkan draft outline metodologi CBI khusus untuk Kota Manado (misalnya data yang dibutuhkan, sumber, dan langkah analisis) supaya bisa jadi rujukan awal bila ingin menyusunnya?

In 2023, the city's households generated an estimated 3,407,352 tons of CO₂e annually from food consumption, highlighting the urgent need for dietary shifts toward plant-based foods to mitigate environmental impact. Additionally, the substantial food waste of 23,658 tons per year — caused by impulsive shopping, poor meal planning, and improper storage — results in greenhouse gas emissions of 21,055 tons of CO₂e. 
2	Methods
2.1. Household survey using questionnaires
This method was used to collect household information regarding shopping habits, food consumption, and food waste management. To determine the sample size of surveyed households, Yamane's (1967) formula (Equation 1) was used with a default confidence level of 95%.

Where: 
-	n is the sample size.
-	N is the population of Hue City in 2023. 
-	e is the chosen margin of error.
According to the Thua Thien Hue Statistical Yearbook 2024, the total number of households in Hue City (formerly Thua Thien Hue Province) is 284,524 [9]. Applying the above formula with a chosen margin of error of 5%, the calculated sample size was 399 households, rounded up to 400. 
To avoid bias and ensure statistical representativeness of the surveyed households in Hue City, the stratified sampling technique was employed. The entire city of Hue was divided into strata based on geographical characteristics: mountainous areas, plains, and coastal areas. After dividing the population into strata, random sampling was conducted within each stratum: Nam Dong and A Luoi Rural Districts represent the mountainous areas, Thuan Hoa and Phu Xuan Districts stand for the plains, and Phu Loc and Phu Vang Rural Districts typify the coastal region 
The survey targets official members of the households living in the houses surveyed, aged 18 and above, who are aware of the subject matter of the survey, actively participating in household food consumption, and can answer the survey questions.
A questionnaire, which acted as a survey instrument, was formulated to collect primary household data. It was pretested on a sample of five households before being administered for data collection.
2.2. Calculation of greenhouse gas emissions
The calculation of GHG emissions related to household food consumption involves a three-step process, considering the entire life cycle of food from production, processing, distribution, to consumption and disposal.
1) Data Collection
Data on the types and amounts of food consumed by households over a defined period (daily or weekly) was obtained through the household survey described above
2) Application of Emission Factors
Each type of food is associated with its corresponding life cycle stages, such as production (cultivation, livestock farming, fishing, etc.), processing (cleaning, milling, canning, etc.), distribution (transportation, storage, retail, etc.), consumption (purchasing, preparation, eating, etc.), and waste management (composting, landfilling, etc.). 
GHG emissions based on the LCA per kilogram (referred to as emission factors) of basic food products, as established by Poore and Nemecek (2018), were used to calculate the GHG emissions of food across all stages of its life cycle.
3) Estimation of greenhouse gas emissions
The emission factor for that item is multiplied by the corresponding quantity consumed to obtain the emissions linked to a particular food item. For each food item consumed by the household over the selected period (day/week/month/year), this method is repeated. The total GHG emissions resulting from a household's food consumption are calculated by summing emissions from all individual food items, as illustrated in formula 2. 
Total GHG emissions = Σ (Emission factor_i * Quantity_i) 	(2)
Where: 
-	i represents each life cycle stage or food item.
-	Emission factor_i is the average GHG emissions per unit for stage/item i.
-	Quantity_i is the amount of food item i consumed.
 2.3. Data Analysis
The data collected from the questionnaire-based interview method and the GHG emission calculations were analyzed using the Data Analysis tool in MS Excel, specifically an add-in called Analysis ToolPak Plus. This tool was used to quickly calculate the mean value and the standard deviation (SD) related to the data.
